 Loyola students express grievances with barriers to absentee voting
 Students outlined their struggles with absentee voting amid the midterm elections.
 By 
 Sara Ketterhagen 
 | November 18, 2026 , 3:15 am 
 Some out-of-state voters at Loyola experienced trouble with absentee voting. (Paige Dillinger / The Phoenix) 
 In the wake of the Nov. 3 election, several Loyola students reported they had issues with receiving or submitting their absentee ballots. 
 Leading up to the election, the Pew Research Center published a report which revealed 25% of voters had already voted absentee by mail or had a plan to and 69% of registered voters were confident in the United States Postal Service’s ability to return ballots on time to be counted. 
 Third-year political science and Spanish major Maggie McGill said her absentee ballot was sent to her parents home in Omaha, Neb. rather than to her apartment in Chicago.
 “I know that I submitted the correct address and then they sent it back to my house in Nebraska,” McGill said. “It was very stressful. The weirdest thing is that in 2024, I had no issues. My ballot arrived in early October, I filled it out and then I dropped it at the mailbox near the Granville stop.” 
 McGill said her mother was visiting from Nebraska and brought her ballot to her, allowing her to cast her vote. 
 “Voting’s always been very important to me and my family. I’ve been going to political advocacy protests and meetings ever since I was little with my parents,” McGill said. “I voted in every election that I’ve been able to.”
 Cameron Gloier, a second-year political science and economics major, said although she was able to vote absentee, the complicated and time-consuming process of voting absentee in Texas nearly prevented her from getting her ballot in.
 In order to vote absentee in Texas, one must first submit an Application for Ballot by Mail (ABBM). There are two options to submit AABM forms — voters can print out the application using a PDF from the website and mail it using their own postage or apply online to have the form mailed to them, according to the Texas Secretary of State website . 
 Gloier chose the latter option and requested the application be mailed to her in early October.
 The deadline for ABBM forms to be received by the early voting clerk in Texas is 11 days before the election, according to the Vote Texas website . Gloier said she didn’t receive her ABBM form until five days after that deadline. 
 “I tried to track down where the form was, there was absolutely no info on it,” Gloier said. “I decided that I wasn’t going to miss voting.”
 Rather than voting by absentee, Gloier made the decision to rent a car and drive down to Texas so she could make her voice heard. She said the trip took over 15 hours, not including breaks. 
 “It’s your civic duty to go vote. I encourage everyone to be registered, to make plans, to go vote, and just take an active role in electing the people who represent you in big and small issues,” she said. 
 Due to the competitive nature of several of the races in Texas, she said she felt it was very important to cast her vote. 
 “It definitely opened my eyes to sort of the injustices and the voter suppression that’s been going on in Texas,” she said. “It’s opened my eyes to how hard it is to vote by mail.”
 First-year psychology and film media major Chidera Ogogor said he’s a registered voter in Texas and encountered similar issues to Gloier. 
 Ogogor said he’s been registered since he turned 18 in February and that he was able to vote with no problems in-person for the primaries.
 Ogogor was able to print out the ABBM using the PDF on the Texas voting website and submit it in October. After submitting the application, Ogogor said he was unable to see the status of the application. 
 “There’s a tracker online to see, is it approved or is it disapproved,” Ogogor said. “But when I checked to see if my mail-in ballot was coming, it wouldn’t allow me to check at all.”
 Ogogor never received his ballot and was unable to vote in the election.   
 For the future, he said there’s more options for people who are out of state to vote more easily through reforms like online voting. He expressed optimism these reforms would be possible, citing how Texas flipped blue in the past election. 
 Ogogor, Gloier and McGill all agreed that voting is a civic duty. 
 “Voting brings the power back to the people,” Ogogor said.
